explanations.explanation: Bronze it is. Goliath, the Philistine champion from Gath, wore a bronze helmet, a bronze coat of mail and bronze armor on his legs, and he carried a bronze javelin slung between his shoulders (1 Samuel 17:5-6). That's a lot of bronze. I can't even get my oven mitts to match.

Iron does show up, but not in the armor. The point of his spear was iron, and it weighed six hundred shekels (1 Samuel 17:7). The helmet, the coat of mail, the leg armor and the javelin were all bronze (1 Samuel 17:5-6).
Gold isn't the answer, friend. The text names bronze for his helmet, his coat of mail, his leg armor and his javelin (1 Samuel 17:5-6). Gold is a fancy guess, but bronze is what the text gives.

explanations.answer: Choose one man to come fight him
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what he asks. Goliath shouts, "Choose one of your men and have him come down against me." It's one man against one man. Then he lays out the stakes: the loser's side becomes the servants of the winner's side (1 Samuel 17:8-9).

explanations.answer: Send their whole army down at once
explanations.explanation: He asks for one man, not the whole army. His words were, "Choose one of your men and have him come down against me." So it's a single man he wants sent down, not a crowd (1 Samuel 17:8).

explanations.answer: Give up and go back home
explanations.explanation: He doesn't tell them to go home. He tells them to choose one man to come down and fight him. Then he lays out the stakes: the loser's side becomes the servants of the winner's side (1 Samuel 17:9).

True. Goliath says, "If he is able to fight me and kill me, then we will be your servants." That's the deal on the table. Then he adds the other side: if he wins, Israel becomes the servants of the Philistines.

It's actually true. Goliath says, "If he is able to fight me and kill me, then we will be your servants." He puts the other side of the bet right after it. If he beats Israel's man, then Israel would be the servants and work for the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:9).

That's what the text says. When Saul, king of Israel, and all the Israelites heard the Philistine's words, they were dismayed and greatly afraid (1 Samuel 17:11). That's the whole camp, from the king on down. Goliath's challenge reached everybody.

explanations.answer: They're angry and ready to charge
explanations.explanation: No charging here. The text says Saul and all the Israelites were dismayed and greatly afraid when they heard the Philistine. Nobody is rushing down that hill. Not yet, anyway.

explanations.answer: They're calm and start making plans
explanations.explanation: Calm would have been nice, friend. But the text says Saul and all the Israelites were dismayed and greatly afraid (1 Samuel 17:11). So calm isn't the word. Dismayed and greatly afraid is.

Youngest it is. Jesse, an old man from Bethlehem, had eight sons, and the text says David was the youngest (1 Samuel 17:12-14). His three oldest brothers had followed Saul. David was last in line, and I spent years at the back of a junk drawer, so I know a little about being at the back.

Close, but he's not fourth. The three oldest sons were Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah, and Jesse had eight sons in all (1 Samuel 17:12-13). The text says David was the youngest, which puts him at the very end of the line.

Not fifth. Jesse had eight sons, and the text says David was the youngest (1 Samuel 17:12-14). Fifth would put him somewhere in the middle, but the text puts him at the very end of the line. That's behind Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah and all the rest.

Forty days. The text says, "For forty days the Philistine came forward every morning and evening to take his stand." Morning AND evening, for forty days. That's a man with a very reliable schedule and a very rude one.

Seven days would have been bad enough, but it went way longer. The text says Goliath came forward every morning and evening for forty days (1 Samuel 17:16). That's morning and evening, day after day. Forty days is a long time to keep showing up.

It was much longer than three. The text says, "For forty days the Philistine came forward every morning and evening to take his stand." (1 Samuel 17:16). That's forty days of morning and evening appearances.

It's false, friend. Jesse doesn't tell David to bring his brothers home. He tells him to take the grain, the loaves and the cheese, check on their welfare, and bring back an assurance from them (1 Samuel 17:17-18). It's a visit and a delivery, not a pickup.

False is right. Jesse, David's father, sends him with roasted grain, ten loaves and ten portions of cheese. He tells him, "Check on the welfare of your brothers and bring back an assurance from them." Nothing about bringing anybody home.

True. David left his supplies in the care of the quartermaster and ran to the battle line (1 Samuel 17:22). Smart man. You don't want to be holding ten loaves and a pile of cheese when the action starts. Then he asked his brothers how they were doing.

It's actually true. The text says David left his supplies in the care of the quartermaster, then ran to the battle line. When he got there, he asked his brothers how they were doing (1 Samuel 17:22). Hands free, and off he went.

explanations.answer: They flee from him in great fear
explanations.explanation: Right. When all the men of Israel saw Goliath, they fled from him in great fear. That's the whole army, not just one nervous soldier. Remember, David has just arrived and is standing right there watching it happen.

explanations.answer: They charge down the hill at him
explanations.explanation: No charging. The text says all the men of Israel saw Goliath and fled from him in great fear. They went the opposite direction. David had just arrived and watched the whole thing.

explanations.answer: They stand still and hold the line
explanations.explanation: Nobody's holding the line, friend. The text says when all the men of Israel saw Goliath, they fled from him in great fear (1 Samuel 17:24). Fleeing is the opposite of standing still. That's what the text tells us they did.

explanations.answer: Great riches and his daughter in marriage
explanations.explanation: That's the offer going around camp. The men of Israel said the king would give great riches to the man who kills Goliath, and he would give him his daughter in marriage (1 Samuel 17:25). That's a very big prize.

explanations.answer: Half his kingdom and a palace
explanations.explanation: That's a big prize, but it's not the one in the text. The men said the king would give great riches and his daughter in marriage to the man who kills Goliath (1 Samuel 17:25). No kingdom, no palace. The text says what it says.

explanations.answer: A seat at the head of his army
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a seat at the head of the army. What the men of Israel said was that the king would give great riches and his daughter in marriage (1 Samuel 17:25). That seat isn't part of the offer they describe.

True. The men said the king would also "…exempt his father’s house from taxation in Israel." That's the winner's whole family house, not only the winner. Riches, a royal marriage AND no taxes. Somebody in that camp must have done the math.

It's true, friend. The men of Israel said the king would "…exempt his father’s house from taxation in Israel." (1 Samuel 17:25). That comes on top of the great riches and the king's daughter. The reward kept getting bigger.

explanations.answer: The armies of the living God
explanations.explanation: That's it. David asks, "Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?" Notice who David says is being defied. He doesn't say it's just Israel's soldiers or the king. He says it's the armies of the living God.

David doesn't say that. His words were, "Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?" He's not talking about Saul's house at all. He's talking about the living God.
Bethlehem is David's hometown, but the elders never come up here. David says the Philistine should not "…defy the armies of the living God?" (1 Samuel 17:26). That's who he says is being defied.

It's false, friend. Eliab, David's oldest brother, heard him and his anger burned against him. He asked, "Why have you come down here?" and said he knew David's pride and wickedness of heart (1 Samuel 17:28). Proud is not what that sounds like.

False is right. When Eliab, David's oldest brother, heard him speaking to the men, his anger burned against David. He said, "I know your pride and wickedness of heart—you have come down to see the battle!" David answered, "What have I done now?" (1 Samuel 17:28-29).

David doesn't drop it. Right after his answer to Eliab, he turned from him toward another and asked about the offer, and those people answered him just as the first ones had (1 Samuel 17:30). He keeps asking. A scolding from his big brother didn't turn him around.

False, and that's the right pick. The text says David turned from Eliab toward another man and asked about the offer again. Those people answered him just as the first ones had (1 Samuel 17:30). He kept on asking.

explanations.answer: To go and fight Goliath himself
explanations.explanation: He sure does. David tells Saul, "Let no man’s heart fail on account of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him!" (1 Samuel 17:32). Quite a day for a shepherd who was sent with supplies for his brothers (1 Samuel 17:17-18).

explanations.answer: To go home and bring more men
explanations.explanation: Not that one. David tells Saul, "Your servant will go and fight him!" (1 Samuel 17:32). He offers to go out and fight the Philistine himself. Bringing more men isn't part of his offer.

explanations.answer: To play the harp for the troops
explanations.explanation: No harp in this scene. The text says David told Saul, "Let no man’s heart fail on account of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him!" (1 Samuel 17:32). He's offering to fight, not to perform.

explanations.answer: You're just a boy and he's a warrior
explanations.explanation: That's Saul's answer. He says, "You cannot go out against this Philistine to fight him. You are just a boy, and he has been a warrior from his youth." Honestly, I get where he's coming from. On paper, it's not a close matchup.

explanations.answer: Take my whole army with you
explanations.explanation: Saul doesn't offer his army. He says, "You cannot go out against this Philistine to fight him. You are just a boy, and he has been a warrior from his youth." His first answer is no.

explanations.answer: Wait for your brothers to decide
explanations.explanation: His brothers don't get a vote here. Saul speaks for himself: "You cannot go out against this Philistine to fight him. You are just a boy, and he has been a warrior from his youth." That's all he says to David at that point.

explanations.answer: Grabbed it by its fur and killed it
explanations.explanation: David says, "If it reared up against me, I would grab it by its fur, strike it down, and kill it." That's a shepherd who takes the job seriously. I flinch when a cookie sheet clangs, so I'm taking notes.

explanations.answer: Climbed a tree until it left
explanations.explanation: No tree climbing in this story. David says when a lion or bear reared up against him, he would grab it by its fur, strike it down and kill it (1 Samuel 17:35). That's quite a job for a shepherd.

explanations.answer: Called the other shepherds for help
explanations.explanation: David doesn't mention any helpers. He says he went after the animal, struck it down and delivered the lamb from its mouth. If it reared up, he would grab it by its fur, strike it down and kill it (1 Samuel 17:34-35).

Right. David says, "The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." Notice who gets the credit. David looks back at what the LORD already did, and that's what he's counting on now.

Not the king, friend. David says, "The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." He's standing in front of Saul, the king, and he still points to the LORD.

No army in that sentence. David says, "The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." He was out with the sheep when the lion and bear came. It was the LORD he points to.

It doesn't work out that way. David strapped his sword over the tunic and tried to walk, but he told Saul, "I cannot walk in these…" and "I am not accustomed to them." So David took them off (1 Samuel 17:39). The text says he wasn't used to the gear.

False is right. David tried to walk in Saul's tunic and armor, and he told Saul, "I cannot walk in these…" and "I am not accustomed to them." So he took them off (1 Samuel 17:39). Sometimes you walk better in your own gear.
Sling. With the stones in his shepherd's bag, David took his staff in his hand and "…with his sling in hand, he approached the Philistine." A staff, a bag and a sling. That's the whole kit.

No sword on this walk. The text says David had his staff, five smooth stones in the pouch of his shepherd's bag, and "…with his sling in hand, he approached the Philistine." (1 Samuel 17:40). The sword he'd strapped on came off with the armor.

The spear belongs to the other fellow. David took his staff, picked five smooth stones, and approached with his sling in hand (1 Samuel 17:40). Goliath's spear shaft was like a weaver's beam (1 Samuel 17:7).
The text gives the reason right away. When Goliath looked at David, "…he despised him because he was just a boy, ruddy and handsome." (1 Samuel 17:42). He looked, he saw David, and he despised him.
Bethlehem never comes up. The text says Goliath "…despised him because he was just a boy, ruddy and handsome." (1 Samuel 17:42). That's the reason it gives.
Not that either. Goliath despised David "…because he was just a boy, ruddy and handsome." (1 Samuel 17:42). The text gives that one reason.

True. Goliath had just asked if he was a dog that David came at him with sticks (1 Samuel 17:43). Then he calls to David, "Come here," and says, "and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and the beasts of the field!" (1 Samuel 17:44). That's the threat he makes.
It's true, friend. Goliath calls to David, "Come here, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and the beasts of the field!" (1 Samuel 17:44). That's the threat he makes.

explanations.answer: That there is a God in Israel
explanations.explanation: That's what David says. He tells the Philistine, "This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand… Then the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel." (1 Samuel 17:46). What the world will know is about God, not about David.

explanations.answer: That David is a mighty warrior
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say that. He says the LORD will deliver Goliath into his hand, and "Then the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel." (1 Samuel 17:46). The spotlight isn't on David.

explanations.answer: That Saul is a great king
explanations.explanation: Saul isn't the point of David's speech. He says, "Then the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel." (1 Samuel 17:46). That's what he wants the whole world to know.

That's David's reason. He says, "…it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and He will give all of you into our hands." He says it to all those assembled there (1 Samuel 17:47). The reason he gives is that the battle belongs to the LORD.
David says nothing like that. His reason is, "…it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s…" (1 Samuel 17:47). The armor isn't his argument.

explanations.answer: Swords belong to the king alone
explanations.explanation: That's not David's reasoning. He says, "…it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s…" (1 Samuel 17:47). The reason he gives is that the battle belongs to the LORD.

Forehead. David "…took out a stone, and slung it, striking the Philistine on the forehead." Then the stone sank into his forehead, and Goliath fell facedown on the ground (1 Samuel 17:49). The text says David did it with a sling and a stone (1 Samuel 17:50). One stone, one shot.
Not the chest. The text says David slung the stone, "…striking the Philistine on the forehead." Goliath had a bronze coat of mail (1 Samuel 17:5), but the forehead is where it hit.
Not the shoulder, friend. The stone struck the Philistine on the forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground (1 Samuel 17:49). That's where the stone landed.
It's false, friend. The text says, "without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him." David did it with a sling and a stone. The sword comes later, and it's Goliath's own.

False, and you got it. "…David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him." There was no sword in his hand when it happened. The sword only came after, when David pulled Goliath's own sword from its sheath (1 Samuel 17:51).
It's false, friend. The text says, "When the Philistines saw that their hero was dead, they turned and ran." (1 Samuel 17:51). No second champion steps up. They ran instead.

False is right. The text says, "When the Philistines saw that their hero was dead, they turned and ran." No second champion, no new challenge. Then the men of Israel and Judah charged after them (1 Samuel 17:52).

explanations.answer: To Gath and the gates of Ekron
explanations.explanation: Yes. They pursued the Philistines "…to the entrance of Gath and to the gates of Ekron." Gath was Goliath's hometown. Philistine bodies were strewn along the Shaaraim road to Gath and Ekron (1 Samuel 17:52).
Jericho isn't in this chase. The men of Israel and Judah pursued the Philistines "…to the entrance of Gath and to the gates of Ekron." (1 Samuel 17:52). That's where the pursuit reached.

explanations.answer: To the banks of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: The Jordan isn't mentioned here. The text says Israel and Judah chased the Philistines "…to the entrance of Gath and to the gates of Ekron." (1 Samuel 17:52). That's how far the chase went.
That's his question. Saul says to Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this young man?" Abner answers, "As surely as you live, O king, I do not know." Even Abner's drawing a blank.
Saul doesn't ask about age. He asks Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this young man?" (1 Samuel 17:55). He wants to know the family.
That's a fair question, but Saul doesn't ask it. He asks Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this young man?" (1 Samuel 17:55). What he wants to know is whose son David is.
Jesse is right. Saul asks, "Whose son are you, young man?" David answers, "I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem…" (1 Samuel 17:58). That's the name David gives.
Eliab is David's oldest brother, not his father. David answers Saul, "I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem…" (1 Samuel 17:58). Jesse is the one with the eight sons.
Shammah is one of David's older brothers, the third son (1 Samuel 17:13). David's answer to Saul is, "I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem…" (1 Samuel 17:58). Jesse is his father.
